questions.stem: India's CURRENT official poverty line (as per TENDULKAR COMMITTEE 2009) is based on:
questions.explanation: INDIA's POVERTY MEASUREMENT — multiple approaches over years. (1) DANDEKAR + RATH (1971) — first study; defined poverty based on calorie intake (2,250 kcal/day rural + urban), expenditure terms. (2) TASK FORCE (Planning Commission 1979) — calorie norms revised: 2,400 kcal RURAL + 2,100 kcal URBAN. (3) LAKDAWALA COMMITTEE (1993) — CPI deflators by state; retained calorie norms. (4) TENDULKAR COMMITTEE (2009, Chair Suresh Tendulkar) — dropped calorie link; ALL-INDIA POVERTY LINE based on MPCE (Monthly Per Capita Consumption Expenditure) @ 2011-12 prices: ₹816 rural + ₹1000 urban per month (~₹27 rural, ₹33 urban per DAY). Broader consumption basket. Used till 2015. 21.9% poverty in 2011-12 (PC 27% rural, 13.7% urban). (5) RANGARAJAN COMMITTEE (2014) — widened poverty line: ₹972 rural + ₹1407 urban (2011-12). 29.5% poverty in 2011-12. But GOVT never formally adopted Rangarajan; Tendulkar still official. (6) NO NEW OFFICIAL LINE since 2011-12 NSSO consumer expenditure survey data; 2017-18 survey SUPPRESSED by govt citing quality issues. 2022-23 HCES (Household Consumption Expenditure Survey) released Feb 2024 + Aug 2024 (full). MULTIDIMENSIONAL POVERTY INDEX (MPI) — developed by OPHI (Oxford Poverty + Human Development Initiative) + UNDP. India uses NITI Aayog's national MPI (since 2021). COVERS 12 INDICATORS across 3 DIMENSIONS: (a) HEALTH (3 indicators: nutrition, child + adolescent mortality, maternal health). (b) EDUCATION (2: years of schooling, school attendance). (c) STANDARD OF LIVING (7: cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account). Deprivation in 1/3 of weighted indicators = MULTIDIMENSIONALLY POOR. India's MPI HEADCOUNT: (a) 2015-16 = 24.85% (NFHS-4). (b) 2019-21 = 14.96% (NFHS-5). 13.5 CRORE Indians lifted out of multi-dim poverty in 5 years. Latest NITI Aayog estimate Jan 2024: 11.28% MPI poor (2022-23). Targets SDG 1 halving national poverty by 2030. GLOBAL COMPARISON (Global MPI UNDP): India still has LARGEST absolute number of poor (~230 million), but trajectory improving. WORLD BANK POVERTY LINES (global): (1) EXTREME poverty — $2.15/day (PPP, 2017 revision); India ~10% (2019-20 estimates). (2) Lower-middle income line — $3.65/day. (3) Upper-middle income — $6.85/day. India has risen from lower-middle to solidly middle-income trajectory. SCHEMES TO REDUCE POVERTY: (1) MGNREGA (2005). (2) PMAY — rural + urban housing. (3) PMJAY / Ayushman Bharat — health insurance ₹5 lakh cover. (4) PM-KISAN — ₹6000/yr farmer income support. (5) PM GARIB KALYAN ANNA YOJANA (GRATIS food 5kg/person/month post-COVID; extended 2023-28 for 80 crore). (6) Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile (JAM Trinity) — financial inclusion. (7) Targeted PDS (Public Distribution System; fair-price shops; 75 crore beneficiaries post-NFSA 2013). (8) NRLM (National Rural Livelihoods Mission — SHGs). (9) UJJWALA — free LPG. (10) JJM — piped water. (11) Swachh Bharat toilets. (12) Saubhagya — electricity. (13) ASPIRATIONAL DISTRICTS PROGRAMME (2018). (14) POSHAN ABHIYAAN (nutrition). India's POVERTY has declined from 40%+ (1990s) to sub-15% (2023) on consumption metric — BIGGEST POVERTY REDUCTION in human history (per World Bank data). ₹816 rural / ₹1000 urban (2011-12 prices); multidimensional metrics used by NITI Aayog since 2021.

questions.stem: PERIODIC LABOUR FORCE SURVEY (PLFS), which replaced NSSO employment-unemployment surveys in 2017, is conducted by:
questions.explanation: PERIODIC LABOUR FORCE SURVEY (PLFS) — India's primary labour force survey since 2017-18. Conducted by NATIONAL STATISTICAL OFFICE (NSO; formerly NSSO — merged with CSO in 2019 to form NSO) under MINISTRY OF STATISTICS + PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (MoSPI). REPLACED earlier NSSO quinquennial rounds (last 2011-12). FREQUENCY: (1) ANNUAL REPORTS (covering rural + urban). (2) QUARTERLY REPORTS (urban only). KEY METRICS: (1) LABOUR FORCE PARTICIPATION RATE (LFPR) — % of POPULATION aged 15+ who are either WORKING or SEEKING work. India 2022-23: ~57.9%; very LOW by global standards (~75% in China, 62% US, 66% UK). Especially low WOMEN LFPR (~37% India vs ~67% China, 56% US). Rising slightly. (2) WORKER POPULATION RATIO (WPR) — % of population aged 15+ who are employed. 2022-23: ~56.0%. (3) UNEMPLOYMENT RATE (UR) = (unemployed / labour force) × 100. 2022-23: ~3.2% overall; but YOUTH (15-29 yrs) UR ~10% (higher). URBAN UR (~5%) > RURAL UR (~2%). FEMALE UR historically higher but narrowing recently. MEASUREMENT approaches: (a) USUAL STATUS — employment status for previous 365 days. (b) CURRENT WEEKLY STATUS (CWS) — status in previous 7 days; more dynamic. PLFS reports both. NEW JOB INDICATORS: (1) FORMAL vs INFORMAL work — PLFS estimates ~85% of India's workforce is INFORMAL (no social security, contracts); only ~15% formal. EPFO (Employees Provident Fund Organisation) + ESIC (Employees' State Insurance Corporation) track formal sector — ~7-8 crore subscribers. (2) SELF-EMPLOYED (~55-58%) + CASUAL labourers (~23%) + REGULAR wage/salaried (~20%). (3) MSME sector employs ~110M; agri ~46% of workforce; services ~32%; industry ~22%. RECENT TRENDS: (1) COVID-19 shock 2020 — UR spiked to ~24% in April 2020 (CMIE data; PLFS less volatile) + quickly recovered. (2) Post-COVID AGRI employment rose (reverse migration during lockdown); since tapered. (3) FEMALE LFPR rose from 22% (2017-18) to 37% (2022-23) — partly due to unpaid domestic + subsistence work being recounted; partly real. (4) Youth unemployment particularly concerning — SKILL GAPS despite degrees. NEW LABOUR CODES: (1) CODE on WAGES 2019. (2) Industrial Relations Code 2020. (3) Social Security Code 2020. (4) Occupational Safety, Health + Working Conditions Code 2020. Amalgamate + modernise 29 old labour laws. Implementation in progress; Rules notified by states. Labour is CONCURRENT list subject. UNEMPLOYMENT TYPES: (1) FRICTIONAL — between jobs. (2) STRUCTURAL — skill mismatch. (3) CYCLICAL — recession-driven. (4) SEASONAL — agri, tourism. (5) DISGUISED — underemployment (too many on same work, common in agri). (6) EDUCATED unemployment — big India problem; degree without skills. Skill India Mission + PMKVY (PM Kaushal Vikas Yojana) + NSDC (National Skill Development Corporation) programmes. Also the MUDRA + Startup India to create jobs. CMIE (Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy) — private think tank; publishes monthly unemployment data; often differs from PLFS (CMIE typically higher). Two private indicators. AGRI → NON-AGRI transition slow in India; China shifted 60%+ in 30 years via manufacturing; India stuck in 'SERVICES-LED' model. annual reports + quarterly (urban); tracks LFPR, UR, WPR + gender-disaggregated data.

questions.stem: HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI), published annually by UNDP, measures:

options.option_text: LIFE EXPECTANCY + EDUCATION (mean + expected years of schooling) + GNI PER CAPITA (PPP); India ranked 134/193 in 2024 HDR

questions.explanation: HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI) — composite statistic of life EXPECTANCY + EDUCATION + PER-CAPITA INCOME; developed by MAHBUB UL HAQ (Pakistani economist) + AMARTYA SEN (Indian Nobel laureate) in 1990 for UNDP HUMAN DEVELOPMENT REPORT (HDR). PUBLISHED ANNUALLY by UNDP. ~190 countries ranked. FORMULA: HDI = geometric mean of 3 dimensional indices: (1) HEALTH — LIFE EXPECTANCY at birth (range 20-85 years). (2) EDUCATION — combines MEAN YEARS of SCHOOLING (adults 25+) + EXPECTED YEARS of schooling (children entering school). (3) INCOME — GNI per capita (in PPP $, natural log used). Normalised 0 to 1. Rankings: > 0.800 = VERY HIGH human development; 0.700-0.799 = HIGH; 0.550-0.699 = MEDIUM; < 0.550 = LOW. HDR 2024 (covering 2022 data, released March 2024): INDIA RANK 134 out of 193 countries with HDI 0.644 (MEDIUM). Previous 132 out of 191 (2021 data, 2022 report). China rank 75 (High, 0.788); Sri Lanka 78; Bangladesh 129; Bhutan 125; Nepal 143; Pakistan 164; Afghanistan 182. TOP: (1) Switzerland 0.967; (2) Norway 0.966; (3) Iceland 0.959; Denmark, Hong Kong, Sweden, Germany, Ireland, Singapore, Australia. BOTTOM: Somalia, South Sudan, CAR, Chad, Niger. INDIA's HDI HISTORY: 1990 = 0.434 → 2022 = 0.644. Steadily rising. Life expectancy rose from 58 → 67+ years; mean schooling 3 → 6.6 years. Better than most SAARC (except Sri Lanka which has long led human development in region). RELATED INDICES: (1) INEQUALITY-ADJUSTED HDI (IHDI) — HDI adjusted for inequality within country; India IHDI = 0.475 (rank drops). (2) GENDER DEVELOPMENT INDEX (GDI) — ratio of female HDI to male HDI; India = 0.852 (high gap). (3) GENDER INEQUALITY INDEX (GII) — India rank 108 in 2022 (out of 166); improvement needed. (4) MULTIDIMENSIONAL POVERTY INDEX (MPI) — India down from 24.85% (2015-16) to 14.96% (2019-21) per NITI Aayog + 11.28% (2022-23). OTHER KEY INTERNATIONAL INDICES: (1) GLOBAL HUNGER INDEX (GHI) — by Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe; India rank 105/127 (2024) — SERIOUS; GoI criticises methodology. (2) WORLD HAPPINESS REPORT — India rank 126/143 in 2024 (declined); Finland #1 (7th yr); US at 23. (3) DEMOCRACY INDEX (EIU) — India 'flawed democracy' rank 41; Norway #1. (4) CORRUPTION PERCEPTIONS INDEX (CPI) by Transparency Intl — India rank 93 in 2023 (score 39/100). (5) GLOBAL INNOVATION INDEX (GII) — India rank 39/132 in 2024 (UP from 81 in 2015; major improvement). (6) EASE OF DOING BUSINESS (World Bank, discontinued 2021 after methodology scandal); revived as B-READY. (7) GENDER GAP INDEX (WEF) — India rank 129/146 in 2024. (8) GLOBAL FIREPOWER INDEX — India rank 4 military strength. (9) NYT's COUNTRY OF YEAR. (10) PRESS FREEDOM INDEX (RSF) — India rank 159/180 in 2024. (11) HUMAN CAPITAL INDEX (World Bank) — India 0.49. (12) PISA (OECD education) — India participated 2009 (Tamil Nadu + Himachal poor ranks); skipping since. India generally shows MIXED picture — economic rise but social indicators lagging; critical EDUCATIONAL + HEALTH investments needed. Medium category.

questions.stem: The GINI COEFFICIENT, measuring INCOME / WEALTH INEQUALITY, ranges from:

options.option_text: 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality — one person has everything); India's income Gini ~0.35-0.40; wealth Gini ~0.83

questions.explanation: GINI COEFFICIENT — most common measure of INCOME + WEALTH INEQUALITY. Developed by Italian statistician CORRADO GINI in 1912 paper 'Variabilità e mutabilità'. RANGE: 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100 if expressed as percentage). (1) Gini = 0 → PERFECT EQUALITY (everyone has same income/wealth). (2) Gini = 1 → PERFECT INEQUALITY (one person has everything, others have nothing). DERIVED from LORENZ CURVE (plot of cumulative income share vs cumulative population share). Gini = area between Lorenz curve + line of equality (45° diagonal), divided by total area below 45° line. INCOME GINI (world): (1) MOST EQUAL — Slovakia 0.23, Slovenia 0.24, Czech Republic 0.25, Denmark, Norway, Netherlands — Nordic + European welfare states. (2) MOST UNEQUAL — South Africa 0.63 (worst among major economies), Namibia, Zambia, CAR, Brazil, Colombia. (3) INDIA income Gini ~0.35-0.38 (relatively modest — but rising). (4) CHINA ~0.46. (5) USA ~0.41. WEALTH GINI (typically much higher than income Gini): (1) INDIA ~0.83 (very high). (2) USA ~0.85. (3) Brazil, South Africa ~0.80-0.85. (4) Most equal — Japan, Scandinavia ~0.60. INDIA's INCOME + WEALTH INEQUALITY: (a) OXFAM 2024 report: TOP 1% of India owns ~40% of national wealth; BOTTOM 50% owns 3%. (b) Billionaire count — India has 185+ billionaires (3rd after US + China). (c) 'Inequality Inc.' report. (d) WORLD INEQUALITY DATABASE (Chancel + Piketty): India's top 1% income share 22% (2022 vs world 11%). (e) Wealth MUCH more concentrated — Ambani + Adani families alone own wealth equivalent to bottom ~10-15% of India's population. DEBATES: (a) POVERTY reduction + inequality rise can co-occur — absolute welfare improves for poor while top gains dominate growth; (b) Rural-urban + caste + gender dimensions of inequality in India; (c) Privatisation + automation may exacerbate. KUZNETS CURVE — Simon Kuznets 1955 hypothesis — inequality rises in early industrialisation, peaks, then falls as country becomes richer. India in rising phase; unclear if will peak + decline. OTHER inequality measures: (1) PALMA RATIO (income share top 10% / bottom 40%) — India ~1.4. (2) 20:20 ratio. (3) THEIL INDEX. (4) ATKINSON index. POLICIES to ADDRESS INEQUALITY: (a) PROGRESSIVE TAXATION (income tax slabs; luxury surcharge). (b) Wealth tax (India abolished 2015; debate continues); (c) INHERITANCE tax (India abolished 1985; Congress 2024 manifesto floated reintroducing; politically fraught). (d) SOCIAL SPENDING — health, education, sanitation, housing, food subsidies. India spends ~2% GDP on health, 3% on education (both below global norms ~6% each). (e) MGNREGA + minimum wages. (f) Direct Benefit Transfer schemes. (g) UNIVERSAL BASIC INCOME (proposed by Economic Survey 2017; Sikkim pilot). (h) Financial inclusion (Jan Dhan + Mudra). (i) Affirmative action — reservation for SC/ST/OBC. (j) Land reforms (pending in many states). (k) Regional balancing — Aspirational Districts Programme. India's challenges: informal labour, low tax-GDP (~12% vs OECD 34%); growing divergence between rich states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, TN, Karnataka) + poor (Bihar, UP, MP, Odisha). highly unequal.

questions.stem: The NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY ACT (NFSA) 2013 provides subsidised food grains to approximately what fraction of India's population?
questions.explanation: NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY ACT (NFSA) 2013 — landmark legislation enshrining FOOD SECURITY as a LEGAL RIGHT. Enacted 12 September 2013 under UPA-II. Aim: 'to provide for food + nutritional security in human life cycle approach, by ensuring access to adequate quantity of quality food at affordable prices'. COVERAGE: UP TO 75% of RURAL + 50% of URBAN population = ~67% overall = ~81.35 CRORE people (out of then 121 cr); currently ~80 cr after Census 2011 base used (needs update post-2021 Census when held). BENEFITS: (1) PRIORITY HOUSEHOLDS (PHH) — 5 KG/PERSON/MONTH of food grains at ISSUE PRICES: ₹3/kg rice, ₹2/kg wheat, ₹1/kg coarse grains. 75% of NFSA beneficiaries are PHH. (2) ANTYODAYA ANNA YOJANA (AAY) — 'poorest of poor' category — 35 kg PER HOUSEHOLD PER MONTH (not per person) at same prices; ~2.3 crore AAY households. (3) MATERNITY — pregnant women + lactating mothers ₹6,000 maternity benefit (PM Matru Vandana Yojana) + take-home rations (1 kg/month) + one hot cooked meal at Anganwadi. (4) CHILDREN — 6 mo to 6 yrs — hot cooked meal/take-home rations at Anganwadi (Integrated Child Development Services, ICDS). Children 6-14 — mid-day meal in schools (PM POSHAN, est 1995; renamed 2021). ELIGIBILITY: States/UTs identify beneficiaries using SECC (Socio-Economic Caste Census) 2011 data + other criteria; cap on eligible population fixed. RATION CARDS updated; BPL / APL distinction obsoleted. IMPLEMENTATION: (1) FAIR PRICE SHOPS (FPS) — ~5.4 LAKH across India; mostly Panchayat/cooperative run. (2) FOOD CORPORATION OF INDIA (FCI, est 1965) — procures, stores, distributes; buffer stocks. (3) CMRs (central pool) + state pools. (4) Food grain procured via MSP at ~23 crops. COSTS: Centre bears ~₹2.1 lakh crore annually for food subsidy (largest budget item after defence + interest + transfer to states). PM GARIB KALYAN ANNA YOJANA (PMGKAY) — launched March 2020 during COVID; ADDITIONAL 5 kg food grains FREE per person over + above NFSA. Continued + extended; now MERGED into NFSA since Jan 2023 — i.e., NFSA allocation FREE (₹0 instead of ₹1-3/kg) till Dec 2028 (5-year extension announced by PM Nov 2023). 81 crore beneficiaries get FREE food grains. ONE NATION ONE RATION CARD (ONORC) — launched 2020; portable ration cards; beneficiaries can access grains anywhere in India via biometric authentication. 100% implementation achieved 2022. Benefits migrants esp. ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) India has been FOOD SURPLUS nation since mid-1970s (Green Revolution). (2) Hunger headcount way down. (3) Maternal + child nutrition improved (but still concerns — stunting 35%, wasting 19% per NFHS-5). CRITIQUES: (1) LEAKAGES — 25-35% historically (reduced with Aadhaar seeding + ePoS machines). (2) INCLUSION / EXCLUSION errors. (3) FISCAL burden high. (4) URBAN poor often excluded. (5) 'Pulses + oils' not covered (only cereals). (6) Inactivity about QUALITY + nutritional adequacy. GLOBAL HUNGER INDEX places India poorly (105/127 in 2024 — 'serious'); GoI disputes methodology. FORTIFICATION: rice fortification under NFSA/PDS (iron + folate + B12) rolled out nationwide by 2024. MILLETS included in NFSA as coarse grains. 75% rural + 50% urban; ~81 crore people eligible; 5 kg/person/month at ₹1/2/3/kg (coarse grains/wheat/rice); world's largest food security programme.

questions.stem: The SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (SDGs) consist of how many goals, set for achievement by 2030?
questions.explanation: SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (SDGs) / 'AGENDA 2030' — 17 INTEGRATED GOALS + 169 TARGETS + 232 indicators, adopted by UN General Assembly on 25 SEPTEMBER 2015 in New York. Timeline: 2016-2030. Replaced MDGs (Millennium Development Goals, 2000-2015 — had 8 goals). ALL 193 UN member states signed. 17 SDGs: (1) NO POVERTY — end all forms globally. (2) ZERO HUNGER. (3) GOOD HEALTH + WELL-BEING. (4) QUALITY EDUCATION — inclusive + equitable. (5) GENDER EQUALITY. (6) CLEAN WATER + SANITATION. (7) AFFORDABLE + CLEAN ENERGY. (8) DECENT WORK + ECONOMIC GROWTH. (9) INDUSTRY, INNOVATION + INFRASTRUCTURE. (10) REDUCED INEQUALITIES — within + between countries. (11) SUSTAINABLE CITIES + COMMUNITIES. (12) RESPONSIBLE CONSUMPTION + PRODUCTION. (13) CLIMATE ACTION. (14) LIFE BELOW WATER (oceans, seas, marine). (15) LIFE ON LAND (terrestrial ecosystems, forests, biodiversity). (16) PEACE, JUSTICE + STRONG INSTITUTIONS. (17) PARTNERSHIPS for the GOALS. Characterised by 'LEAVING NO ONE BEHIND' principle. Universal — applies to ALL countries (developed + developing), unlike MDGs focused on developing. KEY FEATURES: integrated + interconnected; evidence-based; multi-stakeholder (govt + private + civil society + academia). TRACKING: UN Global Monitoring via SDG Indicators Database; annual VOLUNTARY NATIONAL REVIEWS (VNRs) at UN High-Level Political Forum (HLPF). SDG PROGRESS (2024): world LAGGING on most goals; COVID-19 set back progress. Only 17% of targets on track. Climate action + inequality + biodiversity particularly off-track. INDIA + SDGs: (1) NITI AAYOG is nodal agency; tracks via SDG INDIA INDEX (annual since 2018, 5 editions by 2024). (2) LOCALIZATION — state + district-level SDG integration; SDG Cell in every state. (3) 2023-24 SDG India Index: Kerala + Tamil Nadu lead (72 + 71 scores); Bihar + Jharkhand lag (52 + 56). Overall 71/100 for India (Performer category). (4) INDIA's NDC + Panchamrit aligns with SDG 13. (5) Ayushman Bharat + NFSA + MGNREGA + Swachh Bharat align with multiple SDGs. SDG CHALLENGES for INDIA: (a) POVERTY reduction (SDG 1) — achieving with MPI dropping. (b) Hunger (SDG 2) — still major; stunting 35%. (c) Gender equality (SDG 5) — LFPR gap, safety, education gap. (d) Inequality (SDG 10) — rising. (e) Climate (SDG 13) — coal phase-down slow. (f) Biodiversity (SDG 14 + 15) — habitat loss. MDGs (2000-2015): 8 goals — (1) Extreme poverty; (2) Universal primary education; (3) Gender equality; (4) Child mortality; (5) Maternal health; (6) HIV/AIDS, malaria; (7) Environmental sustainability; (8) Global partnership. Mixed but substantial success globally — extreme poverty halved, child mortality down 50%, HIV down; education gains. SDGs DIFFERENCES from MDGs: (a) more numerous + integrated; (b) universal (all countries); (c) covers inequality, climate, cities, oceans (new); (d) includes peace + governance; (e) embraces multi-stakeholder partnership model. POST-2030 discussions already starting — 'Beyond 2030' agenda. Global South concerns: financing gap ($4-7 trillion/year needed vs actual flows), developed country commitment shortfalls, climate finance $100 bn pledge met late + inadequate. UN SDG Summit 2023 midpoint review called for ACCELERATED action.

questions.stem: The 'INDIA'S CHILD STUNTING RATE' according to NFHS-5 (2019-21) is:
questions.explanation: CHILD MALNUTRITION indicators in INDIA (per NFHS-5, National Family Health Survey 2019-21, latest published; NFHS-6 fieldwork underway). (1) STUNTING (LOW HEIGHT-FOR-AGE) = chronic undernutrition: 35.5% of under-5 children stunted (NFHS-5); down from 38.4% (NFHS-4, 2015-16); BIG decline from 48% (NFHS-3, 2005-06) + 52% (NFHS-2, 1998-99). But STILL HIGH by global norms (Africa ~30%, China ~7%). (2) WASTING (LOW WEIGHT-FOR-HEIGHT) = acute undernutrition: 19.3%. (3) SEVERE WASTING: 7.7% (up from 7.5% NFHS-4 — DID NOT IMPROVE; a concern). (4) UNDERWEIGHT (low weight-for-age): 32.1% (vs 35.8% NFHS-4). Overall ~1/3 children chronically undernourished — alarming for a rising economy. GLOBAL HUNGER INDEX 2024: India 105/127 — 'SERIOUS' hunger. GoI disputes methodology. NUTRITION ISSUES: (a) iron-deficiency ANAEMIA — 67% under-5 children, 57% women 15-49, 25% men; MASSIVE burden. (b) Vitamin A, B12, D deficiencies common. (c) STUNTING linked to first 1000 DAYS (conception to 2 years) — irreversible impact on cognitive + physical development. Long-term economic cost: ~2-3% of GDP from lost productivity. GOVT SCHEMES: (1) INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS, 1975) — 14 LAKH Anganwadis (world's largest child nutrition programme); hot cooked meal + take-home rations + preschool + health checkups + immunisation; 8.8 CRORE children covered. (2) MID-DAY MEAL / PM POSHAN (1995, renamed 2021) — free cooked midday meal for Classes 1-8 in govt + aided schools; 11.8 CRORE children covered. TN pioneered (Kamaraj 1956, then MGR expanded 1982). (3) POSHAN ABHIYAAN (National Nutrition Mission, 2018) — 'Nutrition Mission'; aims at reducing stunting by 6% + underweight by 6% by 2022 (targets extended). Integrated approach: ICDS + POSHAN Tracker app + Village Health + Nutrition Days + behaviour change. (4) NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY ACT 2013 — ensures entitlement to food. (5) RAJMATA JIJAU MOTHER-CHILD HEALTH + NUTRITION MISSION (Maharashtra). (6) MAMATA SCHEME (Odisha), Anna Amrutham (Telangana) — state variants. (7) PM MATRU VANDANA YOJANA (PMMVY, 2017) — ₹5,000 maternity benefit for first child + ₹6,000 additional under JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana). (8) ANAEMIA MUKT BHARAT (2018) — iron-folic acid supplementation for 6-groups (kids, adolescents, pregnant, lactating, WRA, men); 6×6×6 strategy. (9) RICE FORTIFICATION in PDS (iron, B12, folate) — rolled out 2022-24. (10) SUPER 75% beneficiaries. GLOBAL benchmarks: WHO 2025 targets = 40% REDUCTION in stunting; India unlikely to meet. India's MATERNAL MORTALITY RATIO (MMR): NFHS-5 — 97/1,00,000 (down from 130 in 2014-16; down from 556 in 1990) — remarkable progress; SDG target 70 by 2030. Kerala has lowest MMR (19); Assam highest (205). IMR (Infant Mortality Rate): 35 per 1000 live births (down from 78 in 1990; 2030 target 12). U5MR: 42 (down from 125). LIFE EXPECTANCY at birth: 70 years (2022, up from 60 in 1990). Major gains but gaps persist. NUTRITION-economic growth PARADOX of India = much-debated (contrast China which reduced stunting from 34% → 7% over same period). still high; down from 38.4% in NFHS-4 (2015-16); reflects chronic undernutrition; stuck despite economic growth.

questions.explanation: INDIA's POPULATION surpassed CHINA's in APRIL 2023 per UN Department of Economic + Social Affairs (UN DESA) estimates — India became the WORLD's MOST POPULOUS COUNTRY. CURRENT (mid-2024): India ~144 crore (1.44 billion); China ~141 crore (1.41 billion, DECLINING); World ~810 crore (8.1 billion, Nov 2022 milestone). India hosts 17.5% of humanity on 2.4% of land area. INDIA's POPULATION HISTORY (Census data): (a) 1901 — 23.8 crore. (b) 1951 (first post-independence census) — 36.1 cr. (c) 1981 — 68.3 cr. (d) 2001 — 102.9 cr (crossed 100 cr). (e) 2011 — 121 cr (LAST CENSUS CONDUCTED). 2021 CENSUS POSTPONED due to COVID + delay continues (pending 2025-26 or later); unprecedented. POPULATION GROWTH RATE: declining dramatically — 2.15% (1981-91) → 1.97% (1991-2001) → 1.64% (2001-11) → now ~1% or less. TOTAL FERTILITY RATE (TFR) — children per woman: (a) 1951: ~6.0; (b) 1991: ~3.8; (c) 2011: ~2.4; (d) NFHS-5 (2019-21): 2.0 — BELOW REPLACEMENT LEVEL (2.1) for first time. Urban TFR 1.6; rural 2.1. STATE-WISE TFR: Sikkim 1.1 (lowest), Goa 1.3, Andaman 1.3, J&K 1.4, Kerala 1.7, TN 1.8, Delhi 1.6, Maharashtra 1.7. HIGH TFR: Bihar 3.0, Meghalaya 2.9, UP 2.4, Jharkhand 2.3, Rajasthan 2.0, MP 2.0. SOUTH + WEST + NE below replacement; NORTH still higher. DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND: India's median age ~28 years; 65% of pop under 35; massive WORKING-AGE population (15-59) — ~62% of total. Advantage for economic growth IF adequate jobs + skills + education. Expected to last 2055-60 before aging begins. CHINA DECLINE: TFR crashed to 1.0 (2023); started declining 2022; Communist Party's 1-Child Policy (1979-2015) aggressive effect now evident. Population to drop to 1 bn by 2080. Many Chinese elderly, labour shortages, care crisis looming. ASIAN TIGERS (Japan, S Korea, Taiwan) similar. INDIA's DEMOGRAPHIC STRUCTURE (2023 estimates): (a) 0-14: 24.9%; (b) 15-64: 68.3%; (c) 65+: 6.8% (growing fast). SEX RATIO (females per 1000 males): (a) 2011 Census: 943 (overall), 919 (child sex ratio 0-6 — decline from 927 in 2001; concerning). (b) NFHS-5: 1,020 (overall, FIRST TIME over 1000 in India's history) + 929 (child sex ratio). (c) Kerala best (1,084); Haryana worst (879). SEX-SELECTIVE ABORTION issue — PC-PNDT Act 1994 (Pre-Conception + Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act) bans sex determination + selective abortion — stringent enforcement. URBANISATION: ~35% URBAN (Census 2011 + projections) vs China's 65% + world avg 55%. Slow urbanisation due to migration flows, push + pull, land laws. STATES by population (2011): (1) UP 199.8M (16.5%, if state = country = 5th largest); (2) Maharashtra 112M; (3) Bihar 104M; (4) WB 91M; (5) MP 72.6M; (6) TN 72M; (7) Rajasthan 68M; (8) Karnataka 61M; (9) Gujarat 60M; (10) AP (undivided) 84M (now AP 50 + Telangana 35). India's + Pakistan's combined population ~166 crore > China's 141 crore. ACTUAL DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND capture demands: EMPLOYMENT generation, SKILLS, education, health, women's participation, urbanisation — India's CHALLENGES. AGEING will be a reality post-2050 — health care systems, pensions, elderly care need preparation. 142.8 crore India vs 142.6 crore China; India is world's MOST POPULOUS country; 17.5% of humanity on 2.4% of land; per UN estimates.

questions.stem: The FIRST FIVE-YEAR PLAN of India (1951-56) was based on the:
questions.explanation: FIRST FIVE-YEAR PLAN of INDIA (1951-56) — first of 12 Five-Year Plans. Launched by PM Jawaharlal Nehru; based on HARROD-DOMAR MODEL (British + American economists' work; focused on SAVINGS + CAPITAL accumulation for growth). FOCUS: AGRICULTURE + IRRIGATION + POWER — critical after Partition (which had put India's food-surplus areas in Pakistan) + famines + refugee crisis. MAJOR PROJECTS + ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) BHAKRA NANGAL DAM (Punjab/HP) — inaugurated 1963 but work in 1st plan; Nehru's 'TEMPLES OF MODERN INDIA'; irrigates 1M hectares of Punjab/Haryana/Rajasthan. (2) HIRAKUD DAM (Odisha, Mahanadi) — world's longest earthen dam; commissioned 1957. (3) DAMODAR VALLEY CORP (DVC 1948) — multi-purpose projects. (4) Community Development Programme 1952 (2 Oct — birthday of Gandhi). (5) National Extension Service 1953. (6) UGC (University Grants Commission) 1953. (7) Five STEEL PLANTS planned (Bhilai + Rourkela + Durgapur realised later). (8) Delhi → Chandigarh as Punjab capital (post 1947 partition, Lahore was lost). GROWTH TARGET 2.1% achieved 3.6% — unexpectedly good. 12 FIVE-YEAR PLANS (1951-2017): (1) 1st 1951-56 (Harrod-Domar, agri + irrigation focus; 3.6% growth). (2) 2nd 1956-61 (MAHALANOBIS MODEL — heavy industry; PSUs born — Steel Authority + BHEL + ONGC + Indian Oil all in this era; Bhilai + Rourkela + Durgapur steel plants; 4.1% growth vs 4.5% target). (3) 3rd 1961-66 (self-sustaining growth; FAILED due to Indo-China War 1962 + 1965 Indo-Pak + severe droughts 1965-66; only 2.4% vs 5.6% target). Three ANNUAL PLANS 1966-69 ('PLAN HOLIDAY'). (4) 4th 1969-74 — Indira's 'GARIBI HATAO'; Bank Nationalisation 1969; BANGLADESH WAR 1971; Green Revolution intensified; 3.3% vs 5.7%. (5) 5th 1974-79 — Emergency era; Minimum Needs Programme; TRUNCATED by Janata Party Govt 1978 for new 'Rolling Plan'. (6) ROLLING PLANS (1978-80, Janata). (7) 6th 1980-85 — Indira returned; IRDP; NREGP (Rural Employment Guarantee predecessor); growth 5.7%. (8) 7th 1985-90 — Rajiv Gandhi; emphasis on productivity + modernisation + TELECOM; growth 6.0%. TWO ANNUAL PLANS 1990-92. (9) 8th 1992-97 — under MANMOHAN-RAO LPG reforms; growth 6.8% (best of any plan till then). (10) 9th 1997-2002 — growth + equity + distributive justice; 5.4% actual. (11) 10th 2002-07 — growth 7.8% + poverty reduction focus; Vajpayee/Manmohan transition. (12) 11th 2007-12 — INCLUSIVE growth; 8.1% actual; financial crisis dampened. (13) 12TH 2012-17 — LAST PLAN ('Faster, More Inclusive + Sustainable Growth'); 8% target; actual 6.9%. PLANNING COMMISSION + FIVE-YEAR PLANS SCRAPPED 2014-15; replaced by NITI AAYOG (1 Jan 2015) + 3-yr Action Agenda + 7-yr strategy + 15-yr vision + annual budgets. MAHALANOBIS MODEL (P.C. Mahalanobis, eminent statistician of ISI Kolkata) — 2-sector (consumer + capital goods) model advocating HEAVY INDUSTRY-first strategy (Soviet-inspired). CRITIQUED for neglecting agriculture + consumer goods. 2nd Plan was INDIA's most distinctive planning moment. OTHER PLANNERS: V.T. Krishnamachari, Charan Singh (critical of industry bias), P.C. Mahalanobis, Tarlok Singh, Asoka Mehta, D.R. Gadgil, K.N. Raj, Jagdish Bhagwati (later critic). PLANNING gave India ~10 MAJOR IITs + IIMs + RECs + AIIMS + ICAR + IISc + CSIR labs + ISRO + DAE + DRDO + DVC + FCI + RBI expansion. Keynesian capital-output-ratio model; focus on AGRICULTURE + IRRIGATION (post-Partition food crisis); Bhakra-Nangal + Hirakud dams.

questions.stem: INDIA is targeting to become a 'DEVELOPED NATION' ('VIKSIT BHARAT') by:
questions.explanation: 'VIKSIT BHARAT 2047' — PM NARENDRA MODI's vision to transform INDIA into a DEVELOPED NATION by 100TH YEAR OF INDEPENDENCE (15 AUG 2047). Announced in his 15 AUG 2022 Red Fort speech; reiterated regularly. 'AMRIT KAAL' — 'era of nectar' — the 25-year period 2022-2047 framed as opportunity. TARGETS (broad, not exhaustive): (1) ECONOMY: GDP to $30-35 TRILLION (from ~$4T in 2024); per-capita income to $20,000+ (from ~$2,700); among top-2 world economies (China rival by 2035; US by 2047). (2) DEMOGRAPHY + EMPLOYMENT: create ~20 CR quality jobs (urban + rural); FORMAL employment 25%+ (from ~15%); harness demographic dividend before ageing begins 2055. (3) EDUCATION + SKILLS: universal literacy; 50%+ gross enrolment in higher ed (from 28%); top-quality universities globally; implement NEP 2020. (4) HEALTH: life expectancy 80+ (from 70); universal health coverage; adequate doctors/1,000; eliminate TB, malaria, HIV. (5) INFRASTRUCTURE: 100% electrification + piped water (largely done by 2024); world-class road + rail + air networks; all villages internet (Bharatnet); smart cities; 500+ mass-transit systems. (6) ENERGY: NET-ZERO by 2070 (COP-26 commitment); 500 GW non-fossil by 2030; 100 GW nuclear; green hydrogen economy; full EV for 2-3-wheelers + buses by 2030. (7) AGRICULTURE: DOUBLE farmer incomes; agri-processing + exports; sustainable farming. (8) MANUFACTURING: 25% of GDP (from 15-16%); PLI sectors (semiconductors, EVs, drones, solar, pharma). (9) SERVICES + TECH: AI + quantum + biotech + space + fin-tech leadership; 10+ CR people working in tech. (10) GOVERNANCE: digital governance; least corruption; top-5 on Human Development Index. (11) POVERTY: MPI poverty <5%; inequality reduced via progressive policies. (12) GEO-POLITICAL: UNSC permanent seat; G3 of G20; $1 trillion exports; STRATEGIC autonomy. CHALLENGES / RISKS: (1) MIDDLE-INCOME TRAP — countries like Brazil, Mexico, S Africa stagnated after reaching $10-15K per capita; can India escape? (2) HUMAN CAPITAL gaps — stunting, literacy gaps, skill deficit; 50% of graduates unemployable. (3) EMPLOYMENT crisis — jobless growth concern; agri employs 46% but 17% of GDP. (4) INEQUALITY + SOCIAL COHESION — caste + religious + regional tensions. (5) CLIMATE vulnerability — heat waves, monsoon shifts, cyclones; coastal cities submergence risk. (6) INFRASTRUCTURE deficit — $1.4 trillion needed over 10 years (NIP). (7) GOVERNANCE — institutional strength, rule of law, judicial efficiency. (8) MANUFACTURING — hasn't grown fast enough; stuck at 15-16% GDP. (9) HEALTH EXPENDITURE only 2% of GDP (vs OECD 8-10%). (10) EDUCATION SPEND 3% (vs needed 6%). INSTITUTIONAL ROADMAP: (1) NITI AAYOG's 'STRATEGY FOR NEW INDIA @ 75' (2018) — 41 chapters covering drivers, infrastructure, inclusion, governance; pre-cursor. (2) INDUSTRIAL POLICY 2024-25 revamped. (3) NATIONAL INFRASTRUCTURE PIPELINE (NIP, 2020) — ₹111 lakh crore projects. (4) PM Gati Shakti — multi-modal transport + logistics integration. (5) DIGITAL INDIA + UPI + Aadhaar + DPI = foundational. (6) SKILL INDIA, Make in India, Startup India, Stand-Up India. (7) STATES' role — cooperative + competitive federalism; state strategies for Viksit Bharat. (8) INTERMEDIATE milestones: $5 TR by 2027, $7 TR by 2030-32, $10 TR by 2035. INDIA has outpaced most emerging economies 2014-24; if current trajectory continues + reforms accelerate, Viksit Bharat 2047 is within reach — but requires sustained effort + good fortune on climate + geopolitics. 100th year of Independence; PM Modi's 'Amrit Kaal' target; requires GDP to reach $30-35 trillion (vs current ~$4T); HCI + infra + jobs + innovation.
